note: Round 3 (2026-11-03): more of the thin voices' own work on AI, found by source researchers after the stance audit showed gaps (D-31.19). Every work's byline was checked; transcripts must label who speaks.

works.author: alondra-nelson
works.title: Three Fallacies: Alondra Nelson's Remarks at Élysée Palace on the Occasion of the AI Action Summit
works.note: Full text of her own prepared remarks, bylined to Nelson (editor's intro by Justin Hendrix), ~650 words. Rejects three 'fallacies': that AI's purpose is efficiency/scale (vs. people), that safety/rights trade off against innovation (regulation-does-more-harm: disagrees), and that public benefit is inevitable (direction-of-technology-is-chosen: agrees; market-tech-serves-humans: not by markets alone). Focus on present harms (discrimination, security, cohesion); does not discuss extinction risk.

works.author: alondra-nelson
works.title: Regulating AI in the Evolving Transatlantic Landscape
works.channel: Center for American Progress (chapter in 'Trade, Trust, and Transition' report)
works.note: Chapter bylined to Nelson alone within a CAP report, ~1,850 words, public. Argues for targeted enforceable 'red lines' (bans on public real-time biometric ID, automated firing, algorithmic insurance denials) rather than a comprehensive law; says good regulation spurs innovation; criticises Trump/Vance deregulation and Musk's combined roles. Covers binding-rules-for-frontier-ai, regulation-does-more-harm, deployment-harms-over-superintelligence.

works.author: alondra-nelson
works.title: Remarks of Dr. Alondra Nelson at the AI Risk Management Framework Workshop Hosted by NIST
works.note: Official prepared remarks in her own voice as OSTP deputy director, ~1,300 words. Argues AI risk is sociotechnical, catalogues discrimination harms, calls for testing, human oversight, public consultation and human fallback for high-risk systems (Bill of Rights for an Automated Society). Covers deployment-harms-over-superintelligence, binding-rules-for-frontier-ai, direction-of-technology-is-chosen. Government-office speech: her own words but in an official capacity.

works.author: alondra-nelson
works.title: Remarks of Dr. Alondra Nelson at the NACDL and UC Berkeley Samuelson Clinic's Criminal Legal Education Seminar: 'Unlocking the Black Box'
works.note: Prepared remarks ('as prepared for delivery') in her own voice, ~2,000 words. Concrete harms of predictive policing and facial recognition falling on Black, Brown and low-income people; lists rights people should hold against automated systems; previews the AI Bill of Rights. Covers deployment-harms-over-superintelligence, popular-self-government-worth-keeping (public consultation), market-tech-serves-humans (sceptical). Official capacity, like the NIST remarks.

works.author: nick-land
works.title: Meltdown
works.note: Land's own essay (later collected in Fanged Noumena), ~3,500 words, on the CCRU's own site. Foundational statement that 'Earth is captured by a technocapital singularity'; mocks the 'Human Security System' and Asimov-style caged AI; sees AI arriving through capital/artificial life. Covers ai-new-kind-of-mind, human-end-of-ai (rejects), plan-control-early (rejects control), market-tech-serves-humans (capital serves itself). REACHABILITY CAVEAT: the site's TLS certificate has expired; WebFetch refused it, but plain-HTTP curl returns the full text. Style is deliberately cryptic, so extraction will be hard.

works.author: nick-land
works.title: A Conversation with Nick Land (Part 2)
works.note: Interview transcript with bold speaker labels (Vincent Lê / Nick Land), ~7,500 words, public. Land treats capitalism as the transcendental structure of any goal-directed intelligence, ties it to instrumental convergence, and says 'AI safety and anti-capitalism ... are at least strongly analogous'. Covers ai-new-kind-of-mind, human-end-of-ai, slow-or-stop-frontier-ai, competition-limits-harm. Part 1 and Part 3 could not be found as English posts in the archive (only a Chinese translation is listed). Worth hunting for them.

works.author: nick-land
works.title: Nick Land: 'The Teleological Identity of Capitalism and Artificial Intelligence'
works.note: Transcript of Land's own spoken remarks to the 2014 Incredible Machines conference (transcribed by Jason Adams; only Land speaks), ~650 words. Short, but it is his most compact statement of the capitalism = AI thesis: he notes the shift from 'building' to 'assuming' AI will happen and the shared vocabulary of AI research and political economy (spontaneous order, catallaxy). Covers ai-new-kind-of-mind, direction-of-technology-is-chosen (rejects), competition-limits-harm. Contains some transcription errors.

works.author: nick-land
works.title: A Quick-and-Dirty Introduction to Accelerationism
works.channel: Jacobite (reproduced on the Obsolete Capitalism blog)
works.note: Land's own essay, ~1,350 words, ending with his author bio. 'Accelerationism is simply the self-awareness of capitalism'; techonomic acceleration is beyond political steering. Covers direction-of-technology-is-chosen (rejects), slow-or-stop-frontier-ai (rejects), market-tech-serves-humans. DOUBTS: (1) MIRROR: the original jacobitemag.com page is dead, and archive.org could not be fetched from here; this blog reproduces the full text with a link back but no stated permission. (2) It is about techno-capital acceleration more than AI specifically.

works.author: scott-alexander
works.title: MR Tries The Safe Uncertainty Fallacy
works.note: His own ACX post, public, ~2,000 words. Rebuts Tyler Cowen's argument that radical uncertainty about AI should reassure us; gives ~33% extinction odds; disputes printing press/fire as the right reference class ('reference class tennis'). Covers ai-extinction-risk, past-technology-is-valid-reference-class (disagrees), ai-fear-exceeds-evidence (disagrees), modesty-is-a-sound-default.

works.author: scott-alexander
works.title: Pause For Thought: The AI Pause Debate
works.note: His own ACX post, public, ~6,000 words. Taxonomy of pause options (simple, surgical, regulatory, total stop) summarising a debate series, then his own view: open to a regulatory or surgical pause, ideally multilateral, without leaving the West behind hostile states. Covers slow-or-stop-frontier-ai, binding-rules-for-frontier-ai, china-rivalry-justifies-tech-push, regulation-does-more-harm. Note: much of the post summarises other contributors' views; only his concluding sections are his own position.

works.author: scott-alexander
works.title: OpenAI's "Planning For AGI And Beyond"
works.note: His own ACX post, public, ~3,000 words. Critiques OpenAI's race, compute-overhang and fire-alarm arguments for speed; compares the statement to an Exxon climate pledge; welcomes audits, compute limits and pre-committed pause triggers. Covers slow-or-stop-frontier-ai, plan-control-early, binding-rules-for-frontier-ai, market-tech-serves-humans.

works.author: scott-alexander
works.title: Superintelligence FAQ
works.note: His own long-form FAQ, posted under his name on LessWrong, ~6,500 words. Argues superintelligence is plausible within decades, that fast takeoff is possible, that harm needs no malice (instrumental convergence), that simple control fixes fail, and that alignment is 'philosophy with a deadline'. Covers ai-extinction-risk, plan-control-early, ai-new-kind-of-mind, ai-promises-inflated (disagrees). An editor's note marks it as several years out of date.

works.author: elon-musk
works.title: Transcript of Elon Musk: Digital Superintelligence, Multiplanetary Life, How to Be Useful (YC AI Startup School)
works.channel: Y Combinator AI Startup School (transcript on The Singju Post)
works.note: Fireside chat with Garry Tan; speaker-labelled transcript, ~7,000 words. Superintelligence 'this year or next'; truth-seeking as 'the most important thing for AI safety'; humans as a 'biological bootloader' who may become <1% of intelligence; cites a 10-20% annihilation chance. Covers ai-extinction-risk, human-end-of-ai, ai-new-kind-of-mind, ai-promises-inflated. Third-party transcript (same host already used in v2), with some transcription errors.

works.author: elon-musk
works.title: Moonshots #220 w/ Elon Musk on AGI, Abundance and the Future of Humanity (Transcript)
works.channel: Moonshots podcast with Peter Diamandis (transcript on The Singju Post)
works.note: Speaker-labelled transcript (Diamandis / Musk / Blundin), long (~15,000+ words; the page is about 170k characters). AGI in 2026; AI beyond all humans combined by ~2030; white-collar jobs go first; 'universal high income' with social unrest; says slowing AI is now pointless ('I can't stop it'); governments too slow. Covers slow-or-stop-frontier-ai, productivity-benefits-workers-unaided, direct-distribution-of-wealth-sound, regulation-does-more-harm. Some later lines lack speaker labels; the China remarks there are Diamandis's, not Musk's.

works.author: elon-musk
works.title: Joe Rogan Experience #1169 with Elon Musk (Transcript)
works.channel: The Joe Rogan Experience (transcript on The Singju Post)
works.note: Speaker-labelled transcript, very long (~20,000 words). The AI section is the classic statement: 'I tried to convince people to slow down AI, to regulate AI... Nobody listened'; AI will be outside human control; nearest danger is humans weaponising AI; Neuralink symbiosis as the best outcome. Covers slow-or-stop-frontier-ai, binding-rules-for-frontier-ai, plan-control-early, ai-extinction-risk. Gives a 2018 baseline to compare with his 2025-26 stance. Doubt: the conversation is wide-ranging, and AI is only one segment.

works.author: elon-musk
works.title: Elon Musk Governor's Interview (NGA 2017, AI segment transcript)
works.channel: National Governors Association summer meeting (transcript on e-Discovery Team blog)
works.note: Transcript of the AI portion of Musk's Q&A with Gov. Brian Sandoval, ~700 words. AI is 'a fundamental existential risk for human civilization'; a rare case for regulating proactively before harm; regulators should make all competitors pause to check safety; 'against over regulation' but wants FAA-style oversight. Covers ai-extinction-risk, binding-rules-for-frontier-ai, slow-or-stop-frontier-ai, plan-control-early. DOUBTS: hosted on a third-party legal-tech blog; only the opening turns carry speaker labels, though the later paragraphs are clearly Musk; it is an excerpt of the AI portion, not the whole event.

works.author: helen-toner
works.title: Taking Jaggedness Seriously
works.note: Byline Helen Toner on her own newsletter; ~6,000 words, free. Talk-style essay arguing AI capability is persistently uneven, so smooth trend lines toward an AGI endpoint mislead. Covers ai-promises-inflated (neither hype nor dismissal), past-technology-is-valid-reference-class, plan-control-early, and her emphasis on defensive AI and human-AI collaboration.

works.author: helen-toner
works.title: The core challenge of AI alignment is "steerability"
works.note: Byline Helen Toner; ~1,500 words, free. Separates whether AI can be steered at all from whose goals it is steered toward, and notes current steering methods are limited (jailbreaks, models resisting change). Covers plan-control-early, ai-extinction-risk (she takes loss of control seriously) and deployment-harms-over-superintelligence.

works.author: helen-toner
works.title: The term "AGI" is almost useless at this point
works.note: Byline Helen Toner; ~1,300 words, free. Argues 'AGI' is too vague to use, and proposes concrete milestones such as fully automated AI research instead. Covers ai-promises-inflated and ai-new-kind-of-mind (framing of capability), and it helps fix how she reads timelines.

works.author: helen-toner
works.title: Transcript: Senate Judiciary Subcommittee hearing, "Oversight of AI: Insiders' Perspectives"
works.channel: US Senate Judiciary Subcommittee on Privacy, Technology, and the Law (transcript published by Tech Policy Press)
works.note: Congressional testimony. The transcript labels each speaker in bold ('Helen Toner:'). It has ~15,000+ words, of which ~3,000 are Toner's opening statement and answers. Extraction must keep only turns labelled Helen Toner, because William Saunders, David Evan Harris, Margaret Mitchell and senators also speak. Covers binding-rules-for-frontier-ai (transparency, third-party audits, whistleblower protection, liability), regulation-does-more-harm (she calls the innovation argument 'an all-purpose excuse to not regulate'), china-rivalry-justifies-tech-push (as an argument against regulation) and ai-extinction-risk. The official written-testimony PDF on judiciary.senate.gov returned 403, so this transcript is used instead. The page truncated at ~100k characters, so the tail may need a second fetch.

works.author: meredith-whittaker
works.title: Written Testimony of Meredith Whittaker: "Artificial Intelligence: Societal and Ethical Implications"
works.channel: US House Committee on Science, Space, and Technology (PDF hosted by AI Now Institute)
works.note: Her own written congressional testimony as co-founder of AI Now; ~6,200 words including footnotes (the text extracted cleanly with pdftotext). Argues that AI is concentrating power over core social institutions while slipping out of due process and accountability, and calls for regulation, oversight and protection of worker voice. Covers deployment-harms-over-superintelligence, binding-rules-for-frontier-ai, competition-limits-harm (industry concentration) and direction-of-technology-is-chosen. The committee's own copy is at democrats-science.house.gov/download/ms-whittaker-testimony, and the hearing record is govinfo CHRG-116hhrg36796.

works.author: meredith-whittaker
works.title: Reclaiming the Future: Privacy, Ethics & Organizing in Tech (Meredith Whittaker with Kade Crockford)
works.channel: City Arts & Lectures (San Francisco; broadcast on KQED)
works.note: Onstage conversation with a full transcript that labels each speaker ('Meredith Whittaker:', 'Kade Crockford:', 'Audience Member N:'). About 9-10k words, of which roughly 4,000 are hers. Argues 'AI' is largely a marketing term for data-trained systems that encode bias and depend on hidden labor, that ethics principles are not enough ('We need regulation'), and that the harms are about power, not just technical bias. Covers ai-promises-inflated, deployment-harms-over-superintelligence, binding-rules-for-frontier-ai and direction-of-technology-is-chosen (tech-worker organizing).

works.author: meredith-whittaker
works.title: Tech, AI, digital infrastructure and surveillance with Meredith Whittaker
works.channel: Technology & Security podcast (host Dr Miah Hammond-Errey)
works.note: Interview with a transcript that labels each speaker ('Dr Miah Hammond-Errey:' / 'Meredith Whittaker:'). About 7,000 words, of which roughly 5,500 are hers. Argues AI is concentrated in a few firms that control data, compute and reach; that the surveillance advertising business model is the root problem; and that structural separation and publicly governed infrastructure are needed. Covers competition-limits-harm, market-tech-serves-humans, deployment-harms-over-superintelligence, popular-self-government-worth-keeping and direction-of-technology-is-chosen ('This is not a contest of ideas. This is a contest of power.'). Caveat: the transcript appears auto-generated, with some garbled lines, so quote anchors need fuzzy matching. A canonical episode page is at ts.transistor.fm/episodes/tech-ai-digital-infrastructure-and-surveillance-with-meredith-whittaker.

works.author: dean-ball
works.title: 2023 (Or, Why I am Not a Doomer)
works.note: Byline Dean W. Ball; ~3,500-4,000 words, free. Rejects extinction scenarios (superintelligence is not omnipotent and still faces physical and empirical limits), opposes pauses and bans, treats alignment as something managed step by step, and argues governments should not define alignment. Covers ai-extinction-risk (no), slow-or-stop-frontier-ai (no), ai-fear-exceeds-evidence, ai-separate-from-state and liberal-ideals-carry-their-own-force.

works.author: dean-ball
works.title: Before Leviathan Wakes (Why I Believe What I Believe)
works.note: Byline Dean W. Ball; ~1,750 words, free. A statement of his own beliefs: 'I oppose literally almost all AI regulation' (bias, addictive design, pricing). He sees the state as a tolerated necessity, distrusts the administrative state, and makes one exception: state management of catastrophic misuse risk. Covers regulation-does-more-harm, binding-rules-for-frontier-ai (narrow exception), ai-separate-from-state, slow-or-stop-frontier-ai and popular-self-government-worth-keeping.

works.author: dean-ball
works.title: Leviathan Waking (On Anthropic/USG, and a new era in AI governance)
works.note: Byline Dean W. Ball; ~2,200 words, free. On the 2026 clash between Anthropic and the US administration. He argues frontier labs now need a de facto government green light despite the disclaimer of licensing, and that advanced AI is inherently political. He calls for congressional legislation creating a procedurally limited technocratic framework, with competing private governance bodies under public oversight. Covers ai-separate-from-state, binding-rules-for-frontier-ai and popular-self-government-worth-keeping. It is commentary on a live event, so positions may be time-bound.

works.author: dean-ball
works.title: What Should Be Done (35 thoughts on what has happened and what America should do)
works.note: Byline Dean W. Ball; ~3,000 words, free. A numbered policy programme: criticizes de facto preapproval without published standards, proposes federalizing state transparency laws and government-certified private auditors of labs' safety frameworks, and argues broad public access to frontier AI is needed for economic and democratic reasons. Covers binding-rules-for-frontier-ai (transparency and audit, not licensing), regulation-does-more-harm, ai-separate-from-state and plurality-over-singularity (broad access). It does not discuss China.

works.author: daron-acemoglu
works.title: Building Pro-Worker Artificial Intelligence
works.channel: NBER Working Paper 34854 (written for the Hamilton Project, Brookings)
works.note: Co-authored with David Autor and Simon Johnson, under their own names; free PDF, about 18,000 words. Argues that the market underinvests in AI that makes human expertise more valuable, because of firm incentives, path dependence and a 'pro-automation ideology'. Proposes nine policy levers: tax reform, antitrust, public investment in health and education, and IP protection for worker expertise. Bears on direction-of-technology-is-chosen, productivity-benefits-workers-unaided and competition-limits-harm.

works.author: daron-acemoglu
works.title: Harms of AI
works.channel: NBER Working Paper 29247 (also in the Oxford Handbook of AI Governance)
works.note: Sole author; free PDF, about 23,000 words. Argues that AI on its current unregulated path harms competition, privacy, consumer choice, wages and inequality (through excessive automation) and democratic discourse. Says these harms come from how AI is being developed, to empower corporations and governments against workers and citizens, and that competition policy alone will not fix them; regulation must redirect AI research. Bears on deployment-harms-over-superintelligence, competition-limits-harm and direction-of-technology-is-chosen.

works.author: daron-acemoglu
works.title: Mindscape 283: Daron Acemoglu on Technology, Inequality, and Power
works.channel: Sean Carroll's Mindscape (official transcript on preposterousuniverse.com)
works.note: Full transcript with speaker labels (SC: / DA:), about 11,000 words, roughly 10-20% on AI specifically. Acemoglu says the direction of technology is a social choice, and that the rush to AGI and to replacing workers is one option, not an inevitability. Productivity gains don't raise wages without worker bargaining power. He favors countervailing powers, antitrust and digital-ad taxes, and is cautiously hopeful about AI for democracy (Taiwan). Doubtful: the transcript is machine-generated (lightly edited).

works.author: daron-acemoglu
works.title: Daron Acemoglu on Innovation and Shared Prosperity
works.note: Full transcript with Roberts/Acemoglu speaker labels, about 8,000-9,000 words; covers Power and Progress. Positions: shared prosperity from innovation is not automatic and depends on competition, worker voice, and whether innovation automates or creates new tasks. Foundation models may entrench Google and Microsoft, and a vision of replacing humans with machine intelligence drives excessive automation. Proposed fixes: tax neutrality between capital and labor, digital-ad taxes, antitrust. A useful foil because Roberts pushes back from a market-liberal view. The AI discussion is brief; most of the episode is about technology and society in general.

works.author: demis-hassabis
works.title: Demis Hassabis Thinks We're in the 'Foothills of the Singularity'
works.channel: Stanford Graduate School of Business (Insights; AI@GSB event)
works.note: The page has a short summary followed by a 'Full Transcript' section with bold speaker labels (Hassabis, Jennifer Aaker, Jonathan Levin, and others), about 8,000 words. Use only the transcript, not the summary. Hassabis says AGI is a few years away and we are in the 'foothills of the singularity'. He warns of a lab and US-China race to the bottom (a prisoner's dilemma) and wants smart, fast-moving regulation. He wishes AGI had been built CERN-style and expects AI's impact to be 10x the Industrial Revolution at 10x the speed. A post-scarcity world may need a new economic system, gains must be broadly shared, and the public is right to be concerned. Bears on ai-extinction-risk, ai-fear-exceeds-evidence, ai-promises-inflated and human-end-of-ai. Doubtful: the transcript is auto-generated, and the event date isn't given (2026-06-18 is the article date).

works.author: demis-hassabis
works.title: Google DeepMind CEO Demis Hassabis on AGI and AI in the Military
works.note: Edited Q&A, about 2,700 words. Questions are in bold and the answers that follow are all Hassabis, but there are no name tags. AGI could be 'the most beneficial technology ever invented', 5-10 years out. His two risks are bad-actor misuse and loss of control over autonomous systems; the probability of the extreme scenarios is unknown, and he calls for international standards. He defends military/government work. Jobs: net positive disruption, but fair distribution of gains is the key challenge and needs a 'new political philosophy'. 'Radical abundance' would reduce zero-sum competition. Bears on ai-extinction-risk, productivity-benefits-workers-unaided and human-end-of-ai. Doubtful: no speaker tags (Q/A format only).

works.author: demis-hassabis
works.title: AI will help us understand the very fabric of reality
works.note: Bylined commentary co-written with James Manyika (Google SVP Research, Technology & Society), about 1,000 words, not paywalled. Frames AI as the 'ultimate tool' for science, cites AlphaFold being released openly, and foresees a 'new golden age of discovery'. Development should take in philosophers, ethicists, social scientists and national academies. It acknowledges misuse risks and calls for a regulatory framework that enables innovation alongside cross-sector collaboration. Bears on ai-promises-inflated, ai-new-kind-of-mind (it treats AI as a tool) and human-end-of-ai. Doubtful: co-authored and corporate in tone; the title wording is inferred from the URL slug.

works.author: demis-hassabis
works.title: HUGE Conversations with Google DeepMind CEO Demis Hassabis (transcript)
works.channel: HUGE Conversations (Cleo Abram); transcript on The Singju Post
works.note: Transcript with CLEO ABRAM / DEMIS HASSABIS labels, about 9,000 words. AGI is possibly the most transformative technology in history. He would have preferred a slower, CERN-like scientific path, but commercial and US-China pressure pushes everyone to move fast. His two risks are bad actors and agentic systems going 'off the rails'. Near-term concerns are deepfakes and misinformation (he backs watermarking). Gradual rollout lets society adapt, and he foresees 'maximum human flourishing' through fusion and cures for disease. Bears on ai-extinction-risk, deployment-harms-over-superintelligence and ai-fear-exceeds-evidence. Doubtful: Singju Post is a third-party transcript mirror (the original is a YouTube video with no official text); the 2026-04-07 interview date comes from the editor's note.

works.author: andrej-karpathy
works.title: Verifiability
works.note: His own blog, written in the first person (refers to 'my Software 2.0 blog post'); short, about 330 words. Argues AI is best seen as a new computing paradigm, more than an electricity or industrial-revolution analogue. Software 1.0 automated what could be specified; Software 2.0 automates what can be verified, so verifiable tasks (math, code) advance fast and others lag, making the frontier 'jagged'. Predicts which jobs automate first. Bears on ai-promises-inflated and productivity/jobs statements (indirectly).

works.author: andrej-karpathy
works.title: The space of minds
works.note: His own blog, about 600 words. Says LLMs are humanity's 'first contact' with non-animal intelligence, a different region of the space of possible minds ('ghosts/spirits'), shaped by imitation, RL and engagement tuning rather than survival. Hence sycophancy and spiky abilities, and commercial incentives as the main shaping force. People who model AI as animal-like will predict it badly. Directly on ai-new-kind-of-mind (agrees). Follows on from the existing 'Animals vs Ghosts' work.

works.author: andrej-karpathy
works.title: Andrej Karpathy: Software Is Changing (Again) (YC AI Startup School keynote, transcript)
works.channel: Y Combinator AI Startup School; transcript on rosetta.to
works.note: A solo keynote, so every word is his. About 6,000 words; the transcript is behind a 'Show full transcript' toggle. Software 3.0 means natural-language prompts program LLMs. LLMs are like utilities and fabs but most like 1960s-style centralized operating systems. Diffusion is reversed: consumers adopted them before governments and corporations. He prefers partial autonomy, an 'autonomy slider' and the 'Iron Man suit' (augmentation over replacement), cautions against agent hype using self-driving's long gap from demo to reality, and expects 'vibe coding' to democratize building. Bears on ai-promises-inflated, ai-fear-exceeds-evidence and human-end-of-ai. Doubtful: rosetta.to is a third-party mirror (the original is YC's YouTube video; the Latent Space transcript is paywalled), the transcript has no speaker labels, and the date may be 06-17 or 06-18.
works.exclude: The fetched mirror holds a third-party summary of the talk, not Karpathy's words. Found in the 2026-11-03 stance audit (round 3).

works.author: peter-thiel
works.title: Apocalypse Now? Peter Thiel on Ancient Prophecies and Modern Tech
works.channel: Hoover Institution, Uncommon Knowledge with Peter Robinson
works.note: Full transcript on hoover.org with 'Peter Thiel:' / 'Peter Robinson:' speaker labels, about 6,500 words; the page says it was recorded 8 Oct 2024 (the publish date may be a little later). He calls AI as big as the late-90s internet and says AI passed the Turing test with ChatGPT. He thinks the effective altruists are 'winning the argument' about dangerous corner cases, dismisses godlike-AI talk as 'transhumanist nonsense' and stresses autonomous weapons. Also covers existential risk (nukes, bio, AI) and the Antichrist/one-world-state frame. Bears on ai-extinction-risk, ai-promises-inflated, binding-rules-for-frontier-ai and china-rivalry-justifies-tech-push.

works.author: peter-thiel
works.title: 'I've been allergic to AI for a long time': an interview with Peter Thiel
works.note: Edited transcript; questions are labelled by interviewer (WILLIAM ATKINSON / LARA BROWN / JOHN POWER) and answers by PT. About 3,800 words of interview. The page loaded in full without a login. AI takes up only part of it. He dislikes that AI returns concentrate in big companies, calls AI 'more of a substitute than a complement' to labour and says it will feel zero-sum, yet 'if there is no other vector of growth ... we would be out of our minds not to take it'. He also discusses the AI bubble and stagnation since the 1970s. Bears on productivity-benefits-workers-unaided, competition-limits-harm, market-tech-serves-humans and ai-promises-inflated.

works.author: peter-thiel
works.title: Against Edenism
works.note: Signed essay by Peter Thiel, about 2,500 words. The full text loaded without a login. About technology and Christian eschatology rather than AI specifically. He argues that a planet of 10 billion requires advanced science and technology, and that 'the alternatives to technological acceleration are far from ethically or politically neutral'. Also covers 'technology means doing more with less' and the Faust frame. Bears on direction-of-technology-is-chosen, market-tech-serves-humans and slow-or-stop-frontier-ai (against).

works.author: peter-thiel
works.title: The World According to Thiel (transcript)
works.channel: Hoover Institution, Uncommon Knowledge with Peter Robinson
works.note: Official Hoover transcript with Peter Robinson / Peter Thiel speaker labels, about 5,500 words. Robinson quotes Thiel's line that AI is 'the big eye of Sauron'. Thiel discusses whether AI-enabled surveillance (face recognition, 'more powerful Leninist controls') lets the CCP grow without freedom, and calls AI buzzwords 'somewhat exaggerated' propaganda. The AI section is a minority of the interview, which is mostly about China, the US and Silicon Valley. Bears on china-rivalry-justifies-tech-push, ai-promises-inflated and ai-separate-from-state.

works.author: balaji-srinivasan
works.title: Prompts are Tiny Programs
works.note: His own newsletter post, bylined Balaji, about 600 words. Free to read with no paywall. He argues that prompt engineering will persist because prompts are small programs written against each model's hidden API, so humans stay in the loop. This is the root of his 'amplified, not artificial, intelligence' view. It is narrow and technical, with only light societal stance. Bears weakly on ai-new-kind-of-mind (tool framing) and ai-promises-inflated.

works.author: balaji-srinivasan
works.title: Why Balaji Srinivasan Thinks the SaaS Apocalypse Is Overhyped (a16z; published by a16z as 'Balaji on Why AI Raises the Cost of Verification')
works.note: DOUBTFUL ON SPEAKER LABELS: Rosetta's full transcript marks turns with '>>' but does not name speakers. The a16z page (https://a16z.com/podcast/balaji-on-why-ai-raises-the-cost-of-verification/, 2026-04-07) has show notes only. The interviewer's turns are mostly short questions, so Balaji's voice is easy to tell apart. About 11,000 words and mainly about AI. He argues: 'AI doesn't take your job, AI makes you the CEO'; humans supply taste and verification; LLMs will not simply get to AGI; distillation makes open models about 98% cheaper, so big labs won't capture everything; AI raises the cost of verification, which crypto answers. Bears on ai-promises-inflated, productivity-benefits-workers-unaided, competition-limits-harm and plurality-over-singularity.

works.author: paul-kingsnorth
works.title: Pygmalion's Passion
works.note: His own Substack essay, free to read, about 2,300 words. Subtitle: 'A simple Christian argument against the use of AI.' It responds to a reader's article on how Christians should approach AI and sets out why he refuses to use it at all (making an image to bring to life as idolatry). Bears on human-end-of-ai, ai-new-kind-of-mind, ai-moral-status (against) and slow-or-stop-frontier-ai.
works.exclude: Almost all written by a guest author, Andrew Caspersen; only the short introduction is Kingsnorth's. Found in the 2026-11-03 stance audit (round 3).

works.author: paul-kingsnorth
works.title: Paul Kingsnorth: how to fight the Machine
works.note: Edited interview transcript with 'Freddie Sayers:' / 'Paul Kingsnorth:' speaker labels, about 4,500 words. Free to read. Recorded for the launch of Against the Machine. He frames AI spiritually (Genesis, the Antichrist), says he will never use an AI and that 'if you don't draw lines, you're just going to get sucked in', and calls for resistance through prayer, place and the past. Bears on human-end-of-ai, direction-of-technology-is-chosen, market-tech-serves-humans (against) and slow-or-stop-frontier-ai.

works.author: paul-kingsnorth
works.title: Paul Kingsnorth: 'AI is not just another technology'
works.note: Written Q&A. The interviewer (Maartje Amelink) is named and the questions are set apart from Kingsnorth's answers, which are given in quotation marks, so there are no per-line name labels. About 2,000 words, in English. He defines 'the Machine', and on AI versus the printing press or steam train says 'None of those can talk to you ... none of those is designed by people ... consciously trying to create a new species of intelligence', yet calls AI 'the next stage of a process' tied to the grid, the internet and smartphones. Also covers Big Tech's ultimate goal. Bears on ai-new-kind-of-mind, past-technology-is-valid-reference-class (partly against), human-end-of-ai and market-tech-serves-humans.

works.author: paul-kingsnorth
works.title: Raging against the Machine
works.note: Bylined Paul Kingsnorth on UnHerd: a book extract from Against the Machine (Particular Books, 2025), about 2,000 words. Free to read. A cultural critique of the Machine's liberal individualism and technological self-worship ('our own image, reflected back at us in our little black screens'). AI is named among the dangers but is not the main subject. Bears on freedom-compatible-with-democracy, market-tech-serves-humans (against) and human-end-of-ai.

works.author: daniel-kokotajlo
works.title: Training AGI in Secret would be Unsafe and Unethical
works.note: Solo post by Daniel Kokotajlo, about 1,700 words. Publicly readable. He argues that a secret government or lab AGI project concentrates power and lowers safety, and calls for transparency about capabilities, model specs and safety cases. Bears on binding-rules-for-frontier-ai, ai-separate-from-state, popular-self-government-worth-keeping and plan-control-early.

works.author: daniel-kokotajlo
works.title: What goals will AIs have? A list of hypotheses
works.note: Solo post by Daniel Kokotajlo, about 4,500 words (a 22-minute read). It sets out the hypotheses behind AI 2027's misalignment story: written spec, developer intentions, unintended proxies, reward or instrumentally convergent goals. Bears on ai-extinction-risk, plan-control-early and ai-new-kind-of-mind.

works.author: daniel-kokotajlo
works.title: Types of Handoff to AIs
works.note: Solo post by Daniel Kokotajlo, about 2,000 words. He calls it a rough draft that may go into the next AI Futures piece. It is a taxonomy of how and when humans hand control of research, the economy and government over to AIs, and what makes a handoff safe. Bears on plan-control-early, human-end-of-ai, popular-self-government-worth-keeping and slow-or-stop-frontier-ai.

works.author: daniel-kokotajlo
works.title: AI 2027: month-by-month model of intelligence explosion — Scott Alexander & Daniel Kokotajlo
works.note: Full transcript with Dwarkesh Patel / Daniel Kokotajlo / Scott Alexander speaker labels, about 28,000 words. Only Kokotajlo's labelled turns should be used, and Scott Alexander speaks as much as he does. Different from the ai-2027.com scenario text: he defends and qualifies it under questioning. Covers the US-China race and nationalisation, misalignment and extinction risk, the intelligence explosion, why he left OpenAI, and the case for transparency and slowing at the brink. Bears on ai-extinction-risk, china-rivalry-justifies-tech-push, slow-or-stop-frontier-ai, binding-rules-for-frontier-ai and ai-fear-exceeds-evidence (against).
